reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours of Soft Tissue and Bone
clinicalPearls: A malignant tumour of smooth muscle differentiation arising most often in the uterus, retroperitoneum, large blood vessels (notably the inferior vena cava), and deep soft tissue of the limbs
Predominantly a tumour of middle-aged and older adults, with uterine disease occurring in women typically around or after the menopause
Retroperitoneal tumours often present late with a large abdominal mass and vague symptoms, while vascular tumours may cause obstruction or oedema
Diagnosis rests on morphology plus smooth muscle immunohistochemistry, including smooth muscle actin, desmin, and h-caldesmon
Genetically complex with highly aberrant karyotypes and frequent TP53 and RB1 pathway alterations rather than a single defining fusion
Wide surgical excision with clear margins is the mainstay of treatment; radiotherapy and multi-agent chemotherapy are used selectively by site and risk
Cutaneous (dermal) leiomyosarcoma is relatively indolent, whereas deep, retroperitoneal, and uterine tumours behave far more aggressively
Staging should include cross-sectional imaging of the primary and chest CT, as haematogenous spread to lung is characteristic
reference.pathophysiology: Leiomyosarcoma arises from smooth muscle or its precursor cells, including the smooth muscle of vessel walls, uterine myometrium, and mesenchymal cells of the retroperitoneum. Unlike translocation-associated sarcomas, it is genomically complex, characterised by widespread chromosomal instability and recurrent inactivation of tumour-suppressor pathways such as TP53 and RB1, which permits unchecked proliferation and impaired apoptosis. The retained smooth muscle phenotype accounts for its immunohistochemical profile, while accumulating genetic damage underlies its capacity for aggressive local growth and haematogenous metastasis, particularly to the lungs.
additionalDifferentials: Leiomyoma and cellular/atypical smooth muscle tumours (including uterine variants)
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI of the primary site to define extent and vascular involvement
Chest CT to detect pulmonary metastases
Whole-body functional imaging in higher-grade or large tumours
Core biopsy with careful tract planning where feasible (recognising some uterine tumours are diagnosed after hysterectomy)
Immunohistochemistry (smooth muscle actin, desmin, h-caldesmon) to confirm smooth muscle differentiation
Echocardiography or dedicated vascular imaging for tumours involving the inferior vena cava or great vessels
redFlags: A large retroperitoneal mass with weight loss or compressive symptoms
Rapidly enlarging uterine mass, particularly around or after the menopause, with postmenopausal bleeding
Lower-limb oedema or Budd-Chiari-like features from inferior vena cava involvement
New respiratory symptoms indicating pulmonary metastases
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on site, tumour size, grade, and completeness of resection; superficial cutaneous tumours have an excellent prognosis, whereas deep soft-tissue, vascular, retroperitoneal, and uterine leiomyosarcomas are aggressive with significant metastatic risk and poorer survival.
pitfalls: Assuming a uterine smooth muscle tumour is benign and using morcellation, which can disseminate an unsuspected sarcoma
Confusing retroperitoneal leiomyosarcoma with dedifferentiated liposarcoma without appropriate immunohistochemistry and MDM2 testing
Underestimating vascular involvement and its surgical implications
Focusing on local control while neglecting pulmonary metastatic surveillance
Overtreating indolent superficial cutaneous tumours as if they were deep high-grade disease
references: WHO Classification of Tumours of Soft Tissue and Bone
Enzinger and Weiss's Soft Tissue Tumors
